newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia steps up war of words over NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Russia steps up war of words over NATO expansion.

text.p: Russian officials, hardening their country's campaign against eastward NATO expansion, demanded on Tuesday the right of veto on major European security issues and said Moscow should be ready to use nuclear weapons if attacked.

President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary joined the verbal offensive, cautioning the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation against offering membership to the three Baltic states on Russia's northwestern border.

The verbal barrage appeared part of a Russian campaign to win concessions from NATO over the Western alliance's plans to take in former communist-ruled countries from eastern Europe. Moscow says such expansion would threaten its security.

NATO is negotiating terms for a special relationship with Russia. But Dmitry Ryurikov, Yeltsin's top foreign policy adviser, denounced NATO's refusal to grant Russia the right to a veto on some security issues as "strange, unjust and wrong".

"Refusal to give Russia this right means actually depriving it of the possibility of taking part in settling European security problems," Ryurikov said during a discussion of NATO enlargement hosted by RIA news agency.
"That is why Russia will remain firmly committed to its positions on that issue," RIA quoted him as saying.

Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the policy-making Security Council, also seemed to touch on Russia's security fears over NATO growth by saying Moscow should should be ready to use nuclear weapons if necessary.

"Naturally we are not talking of a preventive nuclear strike but if an aggressor starts a war against us using conventional weapons, we may respond with nuclear ones," Rybkin told the Rossiiskaya Gazeta newspaper.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky later distanced the Kremlin from Rybkin's remarks.
But he also drew attention to Moscow's concern over NATO expansion, making clear it would be particularly alarmed if the former Soviet republics of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia joined the alliance.

"The Baltic countries' entry into NATO would be a serious barrier between them and Russia and would have an extremely negative impact on prospects for forming a long-term model for constructive cooperation in the region," Yastrzhembsky said.
"Preserving their non-bloc status could create the grounds for mutual steps, include concrete steps, for removing all the Baltic countries' remaining security fears," he told reporters.

The row over NATO enlargement threatens Russia's relations with the West, but Yastrzhembsky held out hope that Yeltsin's summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki next month will be capped by "major agreements".

NATO member states are trying to ease Russia's fears that expansion closer to its doorstep will threaten its security, create new divisions in Europe and give Yeltsin's nationalist and communist opponents ammunition to weaken his grip on power.

Senior U.S., Italian and German officials are due to address those concerns during trips to Moscow in the coming weeks, and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana is touring some ex-Soviet republics to discuss their concerns over enlargement.

Both NATO and Russia hope to reach an agreement forming the basis of a special relationship before a NATO sumit in July at which the alliance is expected to issue formal invitations to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
